items.readable_text:
Content:
Let's think about how to simplify the following:
[MATH: \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)}{\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)}]

Content:
The expression above is a fraction, but there are additional fractions in the numerator and denominator.
Such expressions are called fractions of fractions.
We use parentheses to make it easier to read.

Content:
The trick to working with fractions of fractions is to remember that a fraction represents a division. So, a fraction of fractions is a division of two fractions:
[MATH: \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)}{\left(\dfrac{\color{blue}{3}}{\color{red}{4}}\right)} = \left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right) \boldsymbol{\div} \left(\dfrac{\color{blue}{3}}{\color{red}{4}}\right)]

Content:
Now, recall that dividing by [MATH: \dfrac{\color{blue}{3}}{\color{red}{4}}] is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal [MATH: \dfrac{\color{red}{4}}{\color{blue}{3}}.] We can use this fact to simplify the fraction above:

Content:
[MATH: ((2)/(3)) ÷ ((3)/(4))|=; ((2)/(3)) × ((4)/(3))|=; (2 × 4)/(3 × 3)|=; (8)/(9)]

Content:
Therefore,

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)}{\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)} = \dfrac{8}{9}.]

sections.normalized_html: What is [MATH: \dfrac {\left(\dfrac 1 4\right)} {\left(-\dfrac 3 7\right)}] expressed as a single fraction?
sections.readable_text: What is [MATH: \dfrac {\left(\dfrac 1 4\right)} {\left(-\dfrac 3 7\right)}] expressed as a single fraction?

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, remember that a fraction represents a division. So, a fraction of fractions is a division of two fractions:

[MATH: (((1)/(4)))/((− (3)/(7)))|= (1)/(4) ÷ (− (3)/(7))]

Now, recall that dividing by [MATH: -\dfrac{3}{7}] is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal [MATH: -\dfrac{7}{3}.] We can use this fact to simplify the fraction above:

[MATH: (1)/(4) ÷ (− (3)/(7))|=; (1)/(4) × (− (7)/(3))|=; − (1 × 7)/(4 × 3)|=; − (7)/(12)]

Therefore,

[MATH: (((1)/(4)))/((− (3)/(7)))|= − (7)/(12).]

Notice that we used the fact that a positive number times a negative number gives a negative number.

sections.normalized_html: Simplify [MATH: \dfrac{\left(-3\right)} {\left(-\dfrac 3 5\right)}.]
sections.readable_text: Simplify [MATH: \dfrac{\left(-3\right)} {\left(-\dfrac 3 5\right)}.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, remember that a fraction represents a division:

[MATH: ((− 3))/((− (3)/(5))) = − 3 ÷ (− (3)/(5))]

Now, recall that [MATH: -3 =- \dfrac{3}{1}] and dividing by [MATH: -\dfrac{3}{5}] is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal [MATH: -\dfrac{5}{3}.] We can use these facts to simplify the fraction above:

[MATH: (− 3) ÷ (− (3)/(5))|=; (− (3)/(1)) ÷ (− (3)/(5))|=; (− (3)/(1)) × (− (5)/(3))|=; (3 × 5)/(1 × 3)|=; (15)/(3)|=; 5]

Therefore,

[MATH: \dfrac{\left(-3\right)} {\left(-\dfrac 3 5\right)} = 5.]

Notice that we used the fact that a negative number times a negative number gives a positive number.

items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose we want to simplify a fraction of fractions like [MATH: \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{5}{3}\right)}{4}.] In this case, we have a fraction divided by a counting number. We have two methods available.

Content:
The long way is to write [MATH: 4 = \dfrac 4 1] and then calculate in the same way as we did earlier:

Content:
[MATH: (((5)/(3)))/(4)|=; ((5)/(3)) ÷ 4|=; ((5)/(3)) ÷ ((4)/(1))|=; ((5)/(3)) × ((1)/(4))|=; (5 × 1)/(3 × 4)|=; (5)/(12)]

Content:
A quicker way is to recognize that the result will have the same numerator as the top fraction and that the denominator is just the product of the two denominators:

Content:
[MATH: (((5)/(3)))/(4) = (5)/(3 × 4) = (5)/(12)]

sections.normalized_html: Calculate [MATH: \dfrac{\left(-\dfrac 3 2\right)}{6}.]
sections.readable_text: Calculate [MATH: \dfrac{\left(-\dfrac 3 2\right)}{6}.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
We can use either of the following two methods.

Method 1 - The Long Way

First, remember that a fraction represents a division:

[MATH: \dfrac{\left(-\dfrac 3 2\right)}{6} = \left(-\dfrac 3 2\right) \div 6]

Now, recall that dividing by [MATH: 6] is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal [MATH: \dfrac{1}{6}.] We can use this fact to simplify the fraction above:

[MATH: (− (3)/(2)) ÷ 6|=; (− (3)/(2)) × ((1)/(6))|=; − (3 × 1)/(2 × 6)|=; − (3)/(12)]

Finally, we simplify:

[MATH: - \dfrac{3}{12} = - \dfrac{3 \div 3}{12 \div 3} = -\dfrac{1}{4}]

Therefore, [MATH: \dfrac{\left(-\dfrac 3 2\right)}{6}= -\dfrac14]

Method 2 - The Quick Way

The result will have the same numerator as the top fraction, and the denominator is just the product of the two denominators:

[MATH: ((− (3)/(2)))/(6)|=; (− 3)/(2 × 6)|=; − (3)/(12)|=; − (3 ÷ 3)/(12 ÷ 3)|=; − (1)/(4)]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Let's think about how to simplify the following:
[MATH: \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)}{\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)}]

Content:
The expression above is a fraction, but there are additional fractions in the numerator and denominator.
Such expressions are called fractions of fractions.
We use parentheses to make it easier to read.

Content:
The trick to working with fractions of fractions is to remember that a fraction represents a division. So, a fraction of fractions is a division of two fractions:
[MATH: \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)}{\left(\dfrac{\color{blue}{3}}{\color{red}{4}}\right)} = \left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right) \boldsymbol{\div} \left(\dfrac{\color{blue}{3}}{\color{red}{4}}\right)]

Content:
Now, recall that dividing by [MATH: \dfrac{\color{blue}{3}}{\color{red}{4}}] is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal [MATH: \dfrac{\color{red}{4}}{\color{blue}{3}}.] We can use this fact to simplify the fraction above:

Content:
[MATH: ((2)/(3)) ÷ ((3)/(4))|=; ((2)/(3)) × ((4)/(3))|=; (2 × 4)/(3 × 3)|=; (8)/(9)]

Content:
Therefore,

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)}{\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)} = \dfrac{8}{9}.]

---

[MATH: (((1)/(4)))/((− (3)/(7)))|= (1)/(4) ÷ (− (3)/(7))]

Now, recall that dividing by [MATH: -\dfrac{3}{7}] is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal [MATH: -\dfrac{7}{3}.] We can use this fact to simplify the fraction above:

[MATH: (1)/(4) ÷ (− (3)/(7))|=; (1)/(4) × (− (7)/(3))|=; − (1 × 7)/(4 × 3)|=; − (7)/(12)]

Therefore,

[MATH: (((1)/(4)))/((− (3)/(7)))|= − (7)/(12).]

Item 11 — Tutorial: Dividing a Fraction by a Counting Number

Content:
Suppose we want to simplify a fraction of fractions like [MATH: \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{5}{3}\right)}{4}.] In this case, we have a fraction divided by a counting number. We have two methods available.

Content:
The long way is to write [MATH: 4 = \dfrac 4 1] and then calculate in the same way as we did earlier:

Content:
[MATH: (((5)/(3)))/(4)|=; ((5)/(3)) ÷ 4|=; ((5)/(3)) ÷ ((4)/(1))|=; ((5)/(3)) × ((1)/(4))|=; (5 × 1)/(3 × 4)|=; (5)/(12)]

Content:
A quicker way is to recognize that the result will have the same numerator as the top fraction and that the denominator is just the product of the two denominators:

Content:
[MATH: (((5)/(3)))/(4) = (5)/(3 × 4) = (5)/(12)]

[MATH: (− (3)/(2)) ÷ 6|=; (− (3)/(2)) × ((1)/(6))|=; − (3 × 1)/(2 × 6)|=; − (3)/(12)]

Finally, we simplify:

[MATH: - \dfrac{3}{12} = - \dfrac{3 \div 3}{12 \div 3} = -\dfrac{1}{4}]

Therefore,

Method 2 - The Quick Way

The result will have the same numerator as the top fraction, and the denominator is just the product of the two denominators:

[MATH: ((− (3)/(2)))/(6)|=; (− 3)/(2 × 6)|=; − (3)/(12)|=; − (3 ÷ 3)/(12 ÷ 3)|=; − (1)/(4)]
